title: Authentication and authorization in integrations
task_statement: Give each integration call a verifiable identity and the narrowest access it needs. (Inference: wording from secondary sources)

components.name: Per-user delegation to MCP servers
components.first_principle: A remote MCP server authorizes the call from an OAuth token that the client sends for that server, so the token must name the user.

nodes.label: Your app holds the OAuth flow
Upstream system with its own access list

steps: The app signs the end user in and gets an OAuth access token for the MCP server.
The app puts the token in the authorization_token field of the server definition.
The MCP connector sends the bearer token with each tool call to that server.
A Managed Agents vault holds the credentials of one end user, keyed by mcp_server_url.
Anthropic refreshes the access token when the credential includes a refresh block.
Claude Code signs in from /mcp in an interactive session before a run.
pros: The server receives a token for the user who signed in.
A vault keeps tokens out of each request body.
The MCP connector accepts OAuth Bearer tokens for authenticated servers.
cons: The app owns the OAuth flow and token refresh for the Messages API.
The MCP connector is not eligible for zero data retention.
A vault is scoped to the workspace, so any key with workspace access can use it.
use_when: The server must act for a named person.
The remote server requires OAuth before it accepts a call.
The audit must name the person who asked for the action.
do_not_use_when: The server runs as a local stdio process, because the MCP connector cannot reach it.
A batch job has no human actor and one narrow service identity is enough.
Claude Code runs with claude -p and the server needs a new sign-in.

constraints.choice: Pass each user's token for each server.
constraints.combination: Set a refresh block so Anthropic refreshes the token for long sessions.

constraints.choice: Store one credential for each end user in a vault.
constraints.combination: Use separate workspaces for tenants that must not share keys.

constraints.choice: Use an MCP tunnel for a server in a private network.
constraints.combination: Plan for research preview terms with no uptime commitment.

constraints.choice: Sign in again when the server rejects the stored refresh token.
constraints.combination: Run claude mcp login before a non-interactive run.

components.exam_tie: D3.2. Expect a scenario that asks who the agent acted for. The credited answer uses per-user credentials with a token the server checks, not a shared key. (Inference)
components.trap: A shared service key with a user name in the prompt looks like attribution. The system cannot verify a name that the user typed.
components.decision_rule: Give each server a per-user credential when the audit must name the person who asked.
components.exam_tip: If the scenario offers a session id or a prompt field as identity, reject it.

components.name: Workspace and API key boundary
components.first_principle: A workspace groups keys, members, and limits, and a key scoped to one workspace reaches only that workspace.

nodes.label: API key scoped to one workspace

steps: Create one workspace for each project, environment, or tenant that needs separate limits. (Inference)
Create an API key and scope it to one workspace.
Send the anthropic-workspace-id header with requests from an unscoped key.
Assign the workspace roles that the team needs and no more.
Set spend limits for each workspace in the Console.
Archive the workspace when the project ends, and its keys archive with it.
pros: Separate keys and resources for each project or tenant.
The Claude Code workspace keeps developer traffic apart from other workloads.
Each workspace has its own spend limit.
cons: Each workspace adds setup and role management.
A workspace archive cannot be undone.
The Default Workspace cannot be renamed, archived, or deleted.
use_when: Tenants must not share resources or prompt caches.
One team needs its own spend cap.
Test and production environments need separate keys.
do_not_use_when: One internal script needs one key and no separate limits.
The organization needs more workspaces than the default cap without an account request.
The team needs per-member workspace roles on Claude Platform on AWS, because member management is not available there.

constraints.choice: Use one workspace for each tenant that must not share resources. (Inference)
constraints.combination: Prompt caches stay isolated by workspace on the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, and Microsoft Foundry.

constraints.choice: Set a monthly spend limit for each workspace.
constraints.combination: Keep each workspace limit below the tier spend cap. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Set rate limits for each workspace and model in the Console.
constraints.combination: Check the organization tier limits, which apply at the organization level.

constraints.choice: Grant the least workspace role for each member.
constraints.combination: Use the Workspace Limited Developer role when the member needs no tracing views.

constraints.choice: Bind each Claude Platform on AWS workspace to one region.
constraints.combination: Call the workspace only through its region endpoint.

components.exam_tie: D3.2. Expect a scenario with shared keys across teams or tenants. The credited answer scopes keys and workspaces to the boundary that owns the data. (Inference)
components.trap: An unscoped key with a workspace header looks isolated. The key still reaches every workspace that its user or service account can access.
components.decision_rule: Scope the key to the one workspace that owns the data, and give members the least role.
components.exam_tip: A key scoped to one workspace cannot reach another workspace, even with a header that names it.

components.name: Cloud platform identity
components.first_principle: Each cloud platform checks its own identity and IAM policy before it runs a request, so the policy becomes the access control.

nodes.label: Your app with the Anthropic SDK
IAM policy on workspace or deployment

steps: The SDK loads AWS credentials from the default credential provider chain.
The SDK signs each request with SigV4 for the workspace region.
IAM checks aws-external-anthropic:CreateInference on the workspace ARN.
Add aws-external-anthropic:CallWithBearerToken only for API key calls.
Enable outbound web identity federation once for each AWS account.
Use the AWS request ID to look up the call in CloudTrail.
pros: Current IAM roles, policies, and audit tools apply to the calls.
Each workspace has its own ARN for access policy.
Temporary credentials from the cloud identity service limit exposure.
cons: Outbound web identity federation is disabled by default, and every request fails until you enable it.
OAuth is not supported on Claude Platform on AWS.
The Bedrock service role path needs iam:PassRole on the service role ARN.
use_when: The organization manages access with AWS IAM roles and policies.
The organization manages access with Entra ID roles on a Foundry deployment.
Access must be limited to one workspace or deployment.
do_not_use_when: The workload needs user consent through OAuth on Claude Platform on AWS.
The workload would use a long-term Bedrock key. The docs show a deny policy that blocks long-term keys.
The workload runs on Google managed Claude with no IAM role for predict calls.

constraints.choice: Grant access with IAM policies on the workspace ARN.
constraints.combination: Use an API key for a CI job only with CallWithBearerToken.

constraints.choice: Match the region to the workspace region.
constraints.combination: On Bedrock, AWS is the inference data processor, not Anthropic.

constraints.choice: Keep the Anthropic request ID for support tickets.
constraints.combination: Keep the AWS request ID for CloudTrail lookups.

constraints.choice: Request a higher tier through your Anthropic account representative on Claude Platform on AWS.
constraints.combination: On Bedrock, request up to 5 million input TPM without Anthropic approval.

native_services.text: Authentication uses SigV4 or an API key from the AWS Console. Outbound web identity federation must be enabled once per account.
Access uses a Bedrock service role, IAM assumed roles, or bearer tokens. Assumed roles and bearer tokens have a 12-hour maximum.
Access management uses Azure-issued API keys or Entra ID role-based access control.

components.exam_tie: D3.2. Expect a scenario that names a cloud platform and asks how to control access. The credited answer uses that platform identity model and a scoped policy. (Inference)
components.trap: A long-lived static key in code looks simpler. It bypasses the platform identity, so the IAM policy cannot scope or revoke each caller.
components.decision_rule: Use the platform identity and scope the IAM policy to the workspace or deployment.
components.exam_tip: If the scenario needs OAuth user consent on Claude Platform on AWS, reject that option because OAuth is not supported.

decision_flow:
flowchart TD
  A{Must the audit name the human?} -->|No| B{Is the caller a batch or service job?}
  A -->|Yes| C{Does the server need OAuth?}
  C -->|Yes| D[Per-user token in authorization_token]
  C -->|No| E[Per-user vault credential or narrow key]
  B -->|Yes| F[Narrow service identity in one workspace]
  B -->|No| G{Which platform hosts the model?}
  G -->|Claude Platform on AWS| H[SigV4 with IAM policy on workspace ARN]
  G -->|Bedrock| K[Service role or assumed IAM role]
  G -->|Foundry or Google| I[Entra ID or Google IAM role]
  D --> J[Server checks the token for each call]
  E --> J
cheatsheet:
flowchart LR
  I[Identity per hop] --> U[Per-user token]
  I --> V[Vault per end user]
  I --> W[Workspace key scope]
  I --> P[Platform IAM policy]
  U --> S[Server checks token]
  W --> R[Least workspace role]
  P --> A[SigV4 on AWS]
  I --> X[Session id is not identity]
